name: Valley Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of Valley Colliery, on the train's {side}, a coal mine opened in 1874 at the foot of the Hednesford Hills. It worked for 108 years, supplying coal to Rugeley Power Station among others, and some of its buildings now house the Museum of Cannock Chase.

name: St Luke's Church, Cannock
text: Your train passes near St Luke's Church in Cannock, on the train's {side}, a parish church dating from the 12th century. Its nave arcades and tower were added in the 14th century, and two more bays were built at the east end between 1878 and 1882.

name: St Mark's Church, Great Wyrley
text: Your train passes near St Mark's Church at Great Wyrley, on the train's {side}, built in 1845. Its vicar from 1875, Shapurji Edalji, was the first South Asian vicar of any Church of England parish; his son George, wrongly convicted of injuring a pony, was cleared after Sir Arthur Conan Doyle took up his case.

name: Landywood
text: Your train passes Landywood, on the train's {side}, part of Great Wyrley whose name means “the woodland pasture”. In 1945 a Polish Merchant Navy College was set up here in disused Nissen huts.

name: All Saints' Church, Bloxwich
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church in Bloxwich, on the train's {side}, the town's parish church, built between 1791 and 1794 and altered and extended in the 1870s. An 18th-century cross in its churchyard is listed in its own right.

name: The New Art Gallery Walsall
text: Your train passes near the New Art Gallery Walsall, on the train's {side}, designed by Caruso St John after an international competition and opened in 2000. Its stark building was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize that year, and admission is free.

name: Fellows Park
text: Your train passes near the site of Fellows Park, on the train's {side}, home of Walsall Football Club from 1896 until 1990, when the club moved to the Bescot Stadium nearby. Its record crowd was 25,453, for a match against Newcastle United in 1961.

name: Locksmith's House
text: Your train passes near the Locksmith's House in Willenhall, on the train's {side}, a museum in an 1840 house with backyard workshops, typical of the family lock-making businesses that once thrived in the town. The Hodson family made padlocks here, and volunteers show the old skills with the original tools.

name: HM Prison Oakwood
text: Your train passes near HM Prison Oakwood, on the train's {side}, opened in 2012 as the first prison in the UK built in a modular fashion. Planned to hold 2,500 prisoners, it was scaled down to hold up to 1,605.

name: St Peter's Collegiate Church
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Collegiate Church in Wolverhampton, on the train's {side}, much of it 15th-century. For centuries a chapel royal, and from 1480 a royal peculiar independent of the Diocese of Lichfield, it was the only church in Wolverhampton until the 18th century.

name: Monmore Green Stadium
text: Your train passes near Monmore Green Stadium, on the train's {side}, a greyhound track opened in January 1928, which was also home to the Wolverhampton Wolves speedway team. It features in the song “Monmore, Hare's Running” by Half Man Half Biscuit.

name: Boat Gauging House, Tipton
text: Your train passes near the Boat Gauging House at Tipton, on the train's {side}, built in 1873 beside the Birmingham Canal's Main Line. New boats were loaded here with ton weights to measure how low they sat in the water, so that tolls could be charged on their cargo; it was used until 1959.

name: Horseley Ironworks
text: Your train passes near the site of the Horseley Ironworks, on the train's {side}, founded by Aaron Manby and best known for building the first iron steamer, the Aaron Manby, in 1821. It also made many of the canal and railway bridges of the 19th century.

name: Sheepwash Urban Park
text: Your train passes Sheepwash Urban Park, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve of about 37 hectares on land once used for landfill and a brickworks. Redeveloped in the 1980s, it has lakes fed by the River Tame, with islands left as havens for wildlife.

name: Chance Brothers glassworks
text: Your train passes the site of the Chance Brothers glassworks at Spon Lane, on the train's {side}, a pioneer of British glassmaking from 1822. It glazed the Crystal Palace for the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the Houses of Parliament, and made glass for lighthouses.

name: Galton Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Galton Bridge, on the train's {side}, a cast-iron bridge built by Thomas Telford and opened in 1829 to carry a road over the Birmingham Canal's new main line in its deep cutting. When it was built it was reputedly the highest single-span arch bridge in the world.

name: Langley Maltings
text: Your train passes Langley Maltings, on the train's {side}, built in 1898 to supply malt to the Crosswells Brewery nearby. By the end of the 20th century it was one of the few maltings in the country still using the traditional floor malting process; it closed in 2006.

name: Blackheath
text: Your train passes Blackheath, on the train's {side}, which before 1841 was a small group of farmhouses and inns called Bleak Heath. Through the rest of the 19th century it grew into a town for workers in the surrounding industries, such as the coal mine at Coombes Wood.

name: Haden Hill Park
text: Your train passes near Haden Hill Park, on the train's {side}, home of the Haden family for centuries, with the 16th- and 17th-century Haden Hall and the Victorian Haden Hill House. The local council bought it in 1922 after a public subscription and opened it to everyone.

name: Lye
text: Your train passes Lye, on the train's {side}, once famous for making nails, anvils, chains and firebricks. Lye Waste, beside the old village, was common land settled by people who built a house with a fireplace within 24 hours, using mud and clay, to claim it.

name: Stambermill Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the River Stour on Stambermill Viaduct, one of three similar viaducts Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed between Kidderminster and Stourbridge. Built in timber in 1852 to save costs, it was rebuilt in brick 30 years later and has ten arches.

name: Pedmore
text: Your train passes Pedmore, on the train's {side}, a village in the Worcestershire countryside until housebuilding between the wars gradually merged it into Stourbridge.

name: Churchill Forge Mill
text: Your train passes near Churchill Forge Mill, on the train's {side}, one of the last water-powered forge mills left intact in the UK. A mill here is first recorded in a charter of 1238, and part of the site has been restored to working order.

name: Severn Valley Railway
text: Your train passes near Kidderminster Town station, on the train's {side}, one end of the Severn Valley Railway, a heritage line running 16 miles to Bridgnorth. Its steam and heritage diesel trains follow the River Severn for much of the way.

name: Aggborough Stadium
text: Your train passes near Aggborough Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Kidderminster Harriers, opened in 1890. In 1955 it became the first ground to host a floodlit FA Cup match.

name: Droitwich brine springs
text: Your train passes near Droitwich, on the train's {side}, whose natural brine is ten times saltier than sea water, rivalled only by the Dead Sea. Salt was made here by the Romans and through the Middle Ages, from brine that rose to the surface beside the River Salwarpe.

name: Chateau Impney
text: Your train passes near Chateau Impney, on the train's {side}, a house in the style of a French château built in 1873 to 1875 for the salt magnate John Corbett, as a gift for his wife, who had grown up in Paris. Nikolaus Pevsner judged it the showiest of Worcestershire's mansions built on industrial fortunes.

name: Stoke Prior
text: Your train passes Stoke Prior, on the train's {side}, where in 1853 John Corbett bought disused salt works and made them the largest in Europe. The tall chimney of the Stoke Salt Works was for many years a landmark.

name: Lickey Incline
text: Your train runs on the Lickey Incline, the steepest sustained main-line railway incline in Great Britain, opened in 1840: for two miles the line rises one foot for every 37.7 feet along. Many trains once needed banking engines to push them to the top; now only the heaviest freight trains do.

name: Longbridge plant
text: Your train passes near the Longbridge plant, on the train's {side}, opened in 1905. By the late 1960s it employed about 25,000 people, building cars including the original Mini; car assembly ended in 2016.

name: St Laurence's Church, Alvechurch
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Laurence in Alvechurch, on the train's {side}. The village's name means “Ælfgyth's church”, after the woman who founded a church on this site in the eighth century.

name: Forge Mill Needle Museum
text: Your train passes near Forge Mill, on the train's {side}, an old iron forge turned needle-scouring mill in 1730 and now a needle museum. In the 1870s the Redditch area made about 3.5 billion needles a year, around 90 per cent of the world's.

name: Austin Village
text: Your train passes near Austin Village, on the train's {side}, built in 1917 for workers at Herbert Austin's Longbridge factory. Its 200 red cedar prefabricated bungalows were imported from the Aladdin Company of Bay City, Michigan, and crossed the Atlantic in wartime.

name: St Laurence's Church, Northfield
text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church in Northfield, on the train's {side}, dating from the 12th century, with some of the finest Early English work in the county and a rare 14th-century timber porch. A gridiron, the symbol of St Laurence's martyrdom, is carved into the stonework of its tower.

name: Kings Norton Stop Lock
text: Your train passes near Kings Norton Stop Lock, on the train's {side}, on the Stratford-upon-Avon Canal by its junction with the Worcester and Birmingham Canal. Built to stop water flowing from one company's canal to the other, it is the only guillotine-gated stop lock on a canal.

name: Cadbury World
text: Your train passes near Cadbury World, on the train's {side}, on the Cadbury company's Bournville factory site. Opened in 1990, it tells the history of chocolate and of the Cadbury business, and has become one of Birmingham's largest attractions.

name: Metchley Fort
text: Your train runs through the site of Metchley Fort, a Roman fort built in about AD 48, soon after the Roman invasion of Britain. It was defended by a turf and earth bank with a timber wall, towers and double ditches.

name: Old Joe
text: Your train passes near Old Joe, the Joseph Chamberlain Memorial Clock Tower at the University of Birmingham, on the train's {side}, the tallest clock tower in the UK. Built between 1907 and 1909 and modelled on the Torre del Mangia in Siena, it was the tallest structure in Birmingham until 1965.

name: Holliday Street Aqueduct
text: Your train passes under the Holliday Street Aqueduct, which carries the Worcester and Birmingham Canal over the line just south-west of Gas Street Basin. It opened in 1881, built by the railway company as it extended its line into New Street station.

name: Library of Birmingham
text: Your train passes near the Library of Birmingham, on the train's {side}, on Centenary Square. Opened in 2013 at an estimated cost of £188.8 million, it has been described as the largest public library in the UK.
